cues.text: Footprints in the Snow
Born in 1902 at Barbastro, in northeastern Spain, Josemaría Escrivá grew up in a devout family whose fortunes suffered when his father's textile business failed, forcing a move to Logroño.
There, as a teenager, he saw the bare footprints of a barefoot Carmelite friar left in the winter snow.
This small, arresting sight convinced him God was asking something specific of him, though he could not yet say what.
Law and the Priesthood Together
Ordained a priest in Zaragoza in 1925, Josemaría continued studying civil law alongside his priestly duties, moving to Madrid in 1927 to pursue a doctorate.

His ministry there brought him into daily contact with the city's hospitals and poorest districts, deepening a pastoral concern for ordinary working people that would come to define his later mission.
A Vision on Retreat
On October 2, 1928 , while making a retreat in Madrid, Josemaría experienced what he described as a sudden, clear divine illumination.

It revealed a new path within the Church: a movement calling ordinary lay Christians, in every profession and walk of life, to seek genuine holiness through their everyday work, rather than leaving secular life for the cloister.
He named this new institution Opus Dei — 'the Work of God.'
War and Growth

Opus Dei grew slowly through the 1930s, its work disrupted by the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War in 1936, during which religious persecution forced Josemaría into hiding in various locations across Spain.
Following the war, the movement expanded steadily, receiving formal Vatican approval between 1947 and 1950.
Decades later, in 1982, it was established by Pope John Paul II as the Catholic Church's first personal prelature — a structure allowing it to operate across ordinary diocesan boundaries worldwide.
A Message for Everyone
Josemaría's central teaching was expressed in his widely read book of maxims, The Way (1934), and in countless retreats and talks.
It insisted that sanctity was not reserved for priests and religious but was equally accessible to laypeople sanctifying their ordinary work, family life, and daily responsibilities.

He followed the Second Vatican Council's deliberations closely, building relationships with many of its bishops as Opus Dei continued its rapid international expansion through Europe and Latin America.
Legacy
Josemaría died suddenly of a heart attack in his study in Rome on June 26, 1975, moments after glancing fondly at an image of Our Lady of Guadalupe .
Canonized in 2002 by Pope John Paul II after one of the shortest waiting periods in modern papal history, he left behind an institution.

Today, it numbers roughly 90,000 members worldwide, still carrying forward his central conviction that God does not call people out of their ordinary lives to find him, but wants to be found within them.
